title: Organizational Values Rarely Change, But How They Apply Might
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Drawing on Jim Collins's Good to Great, this essay argues that enduring organizational values don't need updating over time — what needs to evolve is how those values get applied. Using 'Respect' as a worked example, it contrasts an older application (dignified, courteous interpersonal exchange) with a more contemporary one (inclusion and recognition), noting organizations can pursue both simultaneously. The piece pushes back on critics who claim unchanging values make an organization stodgy, arguing instead that consistency of core values paired with flexible application is what actually produces sustained greatness.
points: Distinguishes between an organization's core values (which should stay stable) and their application (which should evolve with the times).
Uses Jim Collins's Good to Great as the intellectual foundation, citing his claim that disciplined adherence to values matters more than which specific values are chosen.
Illustrates the values-vs-application distinction concretely through 'Respect,' contrasting an interpersonal-courtesy application with an inclusion-and-recognition application.
Rejects the critique that unchanging values necessarily make an organization inflexible or outdated.
Frames the creative work of leadership as finding fresh expressions of stable values, not periodically rewriting the values themselves.
quotes: In his seminal book, Good to Great, author Jim Collins made the case that sustained greatness in companies is rooted in a steadfast adherence to a set of enduring core values.
Collins argued that great companies build a culture of discipline around their values, providing team members with a clear framework from which to operate and make everyday decisions.
But they miss an important point. Great values don’t need to change as long as how they are applied does.

While treating each other with courtesy, dignity, and respect doesn’t go out of vogue, a more contemporary leadership team might apply the value of respect to how to make all team members feel welcome, included, and recognized.

While some expressions will maintain over the life course of an enterprise, others will change to meet the contemporary needs of the organization. In that way, core values stay central, but how they show up may take a new turn now and again.
